mainTopic: רב and the עין הרע; five views of 'כל חלי'; the praise of פת שחרית; measuring land by water; clearing riverbank trees
overview: The amud opens by settling a contradiction in רב's views. He praises land near a city, yet he worries about the עין הרע; the answer is that a wall and a partition around the field protect it. The גמרא then brings five explanations of 'כל חלי' in the פסוק. רב says it is the עין הרע, שמואל the wind, רבי חנינא the cold, רבי יוסי בר חנינא bodily waste, and רבי אלעזר the gall. Each view is tied to that אמורא's wider teaching. A ברייתא then praises פת שחרית, a simple morning meal, and רבה and רבא בר מרי each bring a פסוק as its source. Next, רב יהודה teaches a surveyor to measure carefully, except for the strips of land along a channel or a river. The amud ends with stories about clearing trees from riverbanks for the boat-pullers, and the explanation of the last story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A wall and partition protect the field
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction in רב's views is settled: land near the city is good only when it is protected by a wall and a partition.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. One statement is about a field surrounded by a wall and a partition. The other is about a field without a wall and a partition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a contradiction in רב's views. He praised owning land near a city, but he also worries that people looking at a field will harm it through the עין הרע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both statements of רב stay true, because each applies to a different kind of field. If a wall and a partition surround the field, people cannot easily look at it, so being near the city is a plus. Without that protection, the עין הרע is a real worry.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the formula that opens an answer

steps.whatToRemember: רב's two statements do not clash. A field near the city is good when it is fenced in, and risky when it is open to people's eyes.

phrases.english: This is not difficult:
this is where there surrounds it
phrases.notes: 'It' is the field. This line is about רב's praise of land near the city.

phrases.english: a wall and a partition,
that is where there does not surround it
a wall and a partition.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִּמְהַדַּר לֵיהּ שׁוּרָא וְרִתְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a contradiction raised just before this section, between two statements of רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each statement applies to a different situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב's praise of land near the city clashed with his fear of the עין הרע.
steps.terutzMaskana: Land near the city is fine when a wall and a partition surround it. Without them, the עין הרע is a concern.

steps.title: רב: 'All sickness' means the evil eye
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that 'כל חלי' in the פסוק refers to the עין הרע.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And ה׳ will remove from you all sickness.' רב said: This is the evil eye.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic and quotes a פסוק that promises the removal of 'all sickness.' רב says this sickness is the עין הרע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'כל חלי' sounds very broad, so רב names the main cause of sickness hiding behind it. In his view, the biggest danger to people is the עין הרע. This opens a list of five opinions on the same פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: The evil eye; harm caused by jealous or envious looking

phrases.english: 'And ה׳ will remove from you all sickness,'
phrases.notes: דברים 7:15

phrases.english: Rav said: This is the eye.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is part of the corrected wording. 'The eye' here means the evil eye.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new topic, still about the עין הרע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'all sickness' in the פסוק refers to the עין הרע.

steps.title: רב's graveyard visit shows his view
steps.stepSummary: רב's reading matches his own experience: he found that 99 of every 100 people die from the עין הרע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב follows his own reasoning. רב went to a graveyard and did what he did. He said: Ninety-nine died through the evil eye, and one died in the natural way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב's reading of the פסוק fits what he says elsewhere. After a visit to a graveyard, he concluded that nearly everyone dies from the עין הרע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'רב לטעמיה' means רב is consistent with his other teaching. If 99 out of 100 deaths come from the עין הרע, it makes sense that he sees it as the 'all sickness' ה׳ promises to remove.

keyTerms.meaning: Follows his own reasoning; consistent with his other teaching

phrases.english: Rav follows his own reasoning.
For Rav went up to a graveyard,
did what he did,
phrases.notes: The גמרא keeps this vague on purpose. Somehow he learned how the people buried there had died.

phrases.english: and said: Ninety-nine died through the evil eye,
and one by the natural way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's reading in step 2 by showing it matches his other teaching.
steps.raayaObject: רב's reading that 'כל חלי' is the עין הרע
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's finding at the graveyard that 99 of 100 people die from the עין הרע

steps.title: שמואל: 'All sickness' means the wind
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that 'כל חלי' refers to the רוח (wind).
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: This is the wind.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a second explanation of the same פסוק. He says 'all sickness' means the רוח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל names a different main cause of sickness. For him it is the wind, which gets into wounds and the body.

keyTerms.meaning: Wind or air, here seen as a cause of harm to the body

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: This is the wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the פסוק than רב's in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'all sickness' in the פסוק refers to the רוח.

steps.title: שמואל says everything comes from the wind
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's reading matches his general teaching that all harm comes from the רוח.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל follows his own reasoning, for שמואל said: Everything is through the wind.
steps.whatsHappening: Just as with רב, the גמרא shows that שמואל's reading fits his other teaching: all harm comes from the רוח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שמואל believes every injury becomes deadly because of the wind, it makes sense that he reads 'all sickness' as the wind. This general claim also sets up the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Everything is through the wind; all harm comes from the wind

phrases.english: Shmuel follows his own reasoning,
for Shmuel said: Everything is through the wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports שמואל's reading in step 4 by showing it matches his other teaching.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's reading that 'כל חלי' is the רוח

steps.title: What about people executed by the king?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: people killed by the government clearly did not die from the wind.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to שמואל, there are those killed by the government!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's claim that everything comes from the wind. People executed by the government seem to die from the sword, not from wind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Everything' is a strong word, so one clear case of death without wind would break שמואל's rule. A person executed by the king looks like exactly that kind of case.

keyTerms.meaning: People executed by the government or king

phrases.english: But according to Shmuel: there are those killed by the government!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's general rule from step 5.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person killed by the government's sword dies from the wound itself, so it seems not everything comes from the wind.

steps.title: Without the wind, even they could be healed
steps.stepSummary: Even people killed by the government could have been healed with medicine if not for the wind.
steps.simpleTranslation: These too: if not for the wind, they could make them a medicine and they would live.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. Even a person struck by the government could be cured, and it is the wind that stops the cure from working.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer explains what שמואל means by 'everything.' The wound alone is not what kills. The wind entering the wound is what makes it deadly, so even these cases fit his rule.
steps.whatToRemember: For שמואל, injuries become deadly because the wind gets in. Without it, even a person struck by the government could be healed.

phrases.english: These too,
if not for the wind,
they would make a medicine for them, and they would live.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Executed people die from the sword, not from the wind.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wound could be healed. It is the wind that makes it deadly.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: 'All sickness' means the cold
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא explains that 'כל חלי' refers to the cold.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: This is the cold.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא gives a third explanation of the פסוק. He says 'all sickness' means the cold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the third choice for the main cause of sickness. For רבי חנינא, it is exposure to cold.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said: This is the cold,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third reading of the פסוק, after רב and שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'all sickness' in the פסוק refers to the cold.

steps.title: Everything is from Heaven except cold and heat
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's reading matches his teaching that everything is from Heaven except cold and heat, which people can guard against.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי חנינא said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven, except for cold and heat. As it says: 'Cold and heat are on the path of the crooked one; one who guards his soul will stay far from them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי חנינא's reading fits his other teaching. Everything is decided by Heaven except cold and heat, which a person can protect himself from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in משלי says a careful person stays away from cold and heat. That means these harms are in our hands, not fixed by Heaven. Since people bring this harm on themselves, it fits that רבי חנינא sees cold as a main sickness that ה׳ promises to remove.

keyTerms.meaning: In the hands of Heaven; decided by ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: So far there are three readings of 'כל חלי': רב says the עין הרע, שמואל says the wind, and רבי חנינא says the cold. Each matches that אמורא's own wider teaching. Two more readings follow in steps 10 and 12.

phrases.english: for Rabbi Chanina said:

phrases.aramaic: הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם, חוּץ מִצִּנִּים פַּחִים.
phrases.english: Everything is in the hands of Heaven, except for cold and heat.
As it is stated: 'Cold and heat are on the path of the crooked one;'
phrases.notes: משלי 22:5

phrases.english: 'one who guards his soul will stay far from them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם, חוּץ מִצִּנִּים פַּחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי חנינא's reading in step 8 by showing it matches his other teaching.
steps.raayaObject: רבי חנינא's reading that 'כל חלי' is the cold
steps.raayaSupportSource: His teaching הכל בידי שמים חוץ מצנים פחים, based on משלי 22:5

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר חנינא: the sickness is bodily waste
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא gives another explanation of the 'sickness' in the פסוק: it refers to bodily waste (צואה).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: This 'sickness' is bodily waste.
steps.whatsHappening: After רב, שמואל and רבי חנינא, a new אמורא gives his own explanation of the 'sickness' that ה' promises to remove.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each אמורא picks a different main cause of illness. רבי יוסי בר חנינא says it is the body's waste, like mucus and earwax. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Bodily waste or excrement (here including mucus and earwax)
'This' — pointing back to the word 'sickness' in the פסוק

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
This is excrement.
phrases.notes: 'This' means the 'sickness' in the פסוק that ה' promises to take away.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא אָמַר: זוֹ צוֹאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, competing explanation of the same פסוק, alongside the earlier ones of שמואל and רבי חנינא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'sickness' in the פסוק refers to bodily waste.

steps.title: Support: too much nose and ear waste is harmful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up רבי יוסי בר חנינא with a known teaching that a lot of nose and ear waste is harmful, while a little is healthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: Waste of the nose and waste of the ear — a lot of it is harmful, but a little is good.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי יוסי בר חנינא's reading fits a known teaching about bodily waste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If extra mucus and earwax can harm a person, then bodily waste really can be a source of sickness. This is the same pattern as steps 5 and 9, where each reading is tied to that אמורא's general view.

keyTerms.meaning: A lot of them is harmful
A little of them is good

phrases.english: As the Master said:
Excrement of the nose and excrement of the ear —
phrases.notes: He means mucus and earwax.

phrases.english: a lot of them is harmful, but a little of them is good.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the reading of step 10.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי בר חנינא's claim that 'sickness' means bodily waste.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching of 'מר' that a lot of nose and ear waste is harmful.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: the sickness is the gall
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר gives yet another explanation: the 'sickness' in the פסוק is the gall (מרה).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: This 'sickness' is the gall.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא offers his explanation of the 'sickness' in the פסוק, saying it refers to the מרה (gall).
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר points to an organ inside the body, the gall, as the main source of illness. A ברייתא in the next step will support him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said: This is the gall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another competing explanation of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'sickness' in the פסוק refers to the gall (מרה).

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא also says that 'מחלה' is the gall, and gives two reasons for the name: it sickens the whole body, and 83 diseases depend on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught so in a ברייתא: 'Sickness' is the gall. Why is it called 'sickness'? Because it makes a person's whole body sick. Another explanation: because eighty-three diseases depend on the gall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says exactly what רבי אלעזר said, which supports his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains the name 'מחלה' in two ways. First, the gall makes the whole body sick. Second, the letters of מחלה add up to 83, which is the number of diseases tied to the gall.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was also taught so' — a ברייתא that supports the statement just made

phrases.english: It was also taught so in a ברייתא:
"Sickness" — this is the gall.
phrases.notes: שמות 23:25

phrases.english: And why is it called "sickness"?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהִיא מַחֲלָה כׇּל גּוּפוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם.
phrases.english: Because it makes a person's whole body sick.
Another explanation: "sickness" —
because eighty-three diseases depend on the gall.
phrases.notes: The letters of מחלה add up to 83: מ is 40, ח is 8, ל is 30, ה is 5.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that supports step 12.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's claim that 'sickness' means the gall.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that explains 'מחלה' as the gall.

steps.title: Morning bread with salt and water cancels these diseases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that all 83 gall-related diseases are cancelled by eating bread with salt in the morning and drinking a jug of water.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all of them — morning bread with salt and a jug of water cancels them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a practical health tip: a simple morning meal protects against all these diseases. This also sets up the next ברייתא about the benefits of morning bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After saying that so many diseases come from the gall, the גמרא gives the cure: a plain breakfast of bread, salt and water. This idea of פת שחרית leads straight into a longer list of its benefits.

keyTerms.meaning: Bread eaten in the morning, a morning meal

steps.whatToRemember: There are several views on what the 'sickness' in the פסוק is: עין הרע, the wind, the cold, bodily waste, and the gall. Each view is tied to that אמורא's general teaching about illness.

phrases.english: And all of them —
phrases.notes: He means all 83 diseases that depend on the gall.

phrases.aramaic: פַּת שַׁחֲרִית בְּמֶלַח וְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל מַיִם
phrases.english: morning bread with salt and a jug of water
cancels them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכוּלָּן, פַּת שַׁחֲרִית בְּמֶלַח וְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל מַיִם מְבַטַּלְתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a remedy for the diseases mentioned in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A morning meal of bread, salt and water cancels the diseases that come from the gall.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists the benefits of morning bread
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists thirteen benefits of פת שחרית, covering protection, wisdom, Torah learning, health and family life.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Thirteen things were said about morning bread: It protects from heat, from cold, from winds and from harmful spirits. It makes a simple person wise. He wins in judgment. He merits to learn Torah and to teach it. His words are listened to. His learning stays with him. His body does not give off sweat. He is intimate with his wife, and he does not desire another woman. And it kills the lice in the intestines.
steps.whatsHappening: Following the mention of morning bread, the גמרא brings a related ברייתא that lists its many benefits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list moves from the body (protection from heat, cold and harm), to the mind (wisdom, Torah learning, memory), and then to health and married life. The idea is that a healthy, satisfied person thinks clearly and acts well.

keyTerms.meaning: He is intimate with his wife

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה עָשָׂר דְּבָרִים נֶאֶמְרוּ בְּפַת שַׁחֲרִית:
phrases.english: Thirteen things were said about morning bread:
it protects from the heat and from the cold,
and from the winds and from harmful spirits,
and it makes a simple person wise, and he wins in judgment,
he merits to learn Torah and to teach it,
and his words are listened to,
and his learning stays with him,
and his body does not give off sweat,
and he is intimate with his wife,
and he does not desire another woman,
and it kills the lice in the intestines.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁלֹשָׁה עָשָׂר דְּבָרִים נֶאֶמְרוּ בְּפַת שַׁחֲרִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the morning bread mentioned in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating bread in the morning brings many physical, mental and spiritual benefits.

steps.title: Some add: morning bread removes jealousy and brings love
steps.stepSummary: Some say that morning bread also removes jealousy and brings in love.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: it even takes out jealousy and brings in love.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with an extra opinion that adds one more benefit to the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The יש אומרים goes further than the main list. Beyond health and learning, the morning meal also improves how a person feels toward others: less jealousy, more love.
steps.whatToRemember: פת שחרית, a simple morning meal, is praised for protecting the body, sharpening the mind, helping Torah learning, keeping a marriage healthy, and, according to some, bringing love instead of jealousy.

phrases.english: And some say:
it even takes out jealousy
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording, so the verbs match 'bread' as their subject.

phrases.english: and brings in love.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים: אַף מוֹצִיאָה אֶת הַקִּנְאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds one more benefit to the list in step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Morning bread also removes jealousy and brings in love.

steps.title: רבה asks for the source of a popular saying about eating early
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks רבא בר מרי where the folk saying comes from: sixty runners cannot catch a man who ate in the morning. He also quotes the חכמים' advice to get up early and eat, in summer and in winter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to רבא בר מרי: Where do we learn this thing people say: 'Sixty runners ran and could not catch the man who ate in the morning'? And the חכמים said: Get up early and eat. In summer, because of the heat. In winter, because of the cold.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה asks for a source in the תנ"ך for a popular saying about the power of eating in the morning. This question sets up the answers in the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps praised פת שחרית (morning bread). Now רבה wants a פסוק behind the folk saying and the חכמים' advice. The idea is that a morning meal makes the body strong enough to handle both heat and cold.

keyTerms.meaning: Where does this thing come from? (a request for a source)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבָּה לְרָבָא בַּר מָרִי:
phrases.english: Rabba said to Rava bar Mari:
From where is this thing that people say:
Sixty runners ran
and did not catch up to the man who ate in the morning.
And the Sages said: Get up early and eat,

phrases.aramaic: בְּקַיִץ מִפְּנֵי הַחַמָּה וּבַחוֹרֶף מִפְּנֵי הַצִּינָּה.
phrases.english: in summer because of the heat, and in winter because of the cold.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the praise of morning bread by asking for a פסוק behind it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק that supports the saying and the advice to eat early in the morning.

steps.title: רבא בר מרי brings a verse from ישעיהו
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר מרי answers with ישעיהו 49:10. Heat and sun will not strike them because they will not be hungry or thirsty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written, 'They shall not hunger nor thirst, and heat and sun shall not strike them.' Why will heat and sun not strike them? Because they will not be hungry or thirsty.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר מרי answers רבה's question with a פסוק. He reads it as cause and effect: since they are not hungry, the heat does not hurt them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists not hungry, not thirsty, and not hurt by heat and sun. רבא בר מרי reads the first part as the reason for the second part. Someone who has eaten is protected from the weather, just like the חכמים' advice.

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"They shall not hunger nor thirst
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 49:10

phrases.english: and heat and sun shall not strike them."
Heat and sun shall not strike them —
because they will not be hungry or thirsty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ישעיהו 49:10: not being hungry or thirsty is the reason heat and sun do not harm a person.

steps.title: רבה brings a different verse from שמות
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that he learns it from שמות 23:25 instead. Serving ה׳ means קריאת שמע and תפלה. Blessing your bread and water means bread with salt and a jug of water. After that, sickness is removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You told me it comes from there, but I tell you it comes from here: 'And you shall serve ה׳ your God, and He will bless your bread and your water.' 'And you shall serve ה׳ your God' means קריאת שמע and prayer. 'And He will bless your bread and your water' means bread with salt and a jug of water. From then on: 'And I will remove sickness from your midst.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה offers his own, different פסוק as the source. He reads it as a morning order: first pray, then eat bread and water, and then sickness goes away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the פסוק as three steps in a row: serving ה׳‎ (שמע and תפלה), then bread and water, then health. This brings us back to steps 13 and 14. There the ברייתא explained 'מחלה' in this same פסוק as the gall, and the גמרא said bread with salt and water cancels its diseases.

keyTerms.meaning: You told me from there (meaning a different source)
And I tell you from here (my source is this one)

steps.whatToRemember: The order of the morning: first קריאת שמע and תפלה, then bread with salt and water. After that the promise 'I will remove sickness from your midst' comes true.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַתְּ אָמְרַתְּ לִי מֵהָתָם,
phrases.english: He said to him: You told me it comes from there,
but I tell you it comes from here:
"And you shall serve ה׳ your God
phrases.notes: שמות 23:25

phrases.english: and He will bless your bread and your water."
"And you shall serve ה׳ your God" —
this is קריאת שמע and prayer.
"And He will bless your bread and your water" —

phrases.aramaic: זוֹ פַּת בַּמֶּלַח וְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל מַיִם,
phrases.english: this is bread with salt and a jug of water.
From then on:
"And I will remove sickness from your midst."
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק. It is the 'מחלה' that the ברייתא in step 13 explained as the gall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתְּ אָמְרַתְּ לִי מֵהָתָם, וַאֲנָא אָמֵינָא לָךְ מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק as the source instead of the one in step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמות 23:25: after prayer, bread with salt and water brings the removal of sickness.

steps.title: Measure land carefully because every bit is valuable
steps.stepSummary: A new topic. רב יהודה tells רב אדא the surveyor not to be careless when measuring, because every small piece of land could grow expensive saffron.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said to רב אדא the surveyor: Don't be careless with measuring, because every little bit of land is fit for growing cultivated saffron.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new subject: how carefully a surveyor must measure land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a tiny strip of land has real value, because saffron is a very costly crop. So a mistake in measuring, even a small one, could cause someone a real loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't treat it lightly, don't be careless

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יְהוּדָה לְרַב אַדָּא מָשׁוֹחָאָה:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said to Rav Adda the surveyor:
Don't be careless with measuring,
because every little bit
is fit for growing cultivated saffron.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יְהוּדָה לְרַב אַדָּא מָשׁוֹחָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic, unconnected to morning bread.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A surveyor must measure precisely, because even small pieces of land are valuable.

steps.title: Strips beside a channel or a river need less exact measuring
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה adds two exceptions. The four אמות next to a water channel may be measured loosely. The four אמות next to a river should not be measured at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said to רב אדא the surveyor: The four cubits next to a water channel, you may be easy with them. The ones next to a river, don't measure them at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives exceptions to his rule about careful measuring: strips of land next to water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said every bit of land counts. Now he says the four אמות beside a channel do not need exact measuring. The strip beside a river is not measured at all. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Be easy with them, measure them loosely

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יְהוּדָה לְרַב אַדָּא מָשׁוֹחָאָה:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said to Rav Adda the surveyor:
The four cubits next to a water channel — you may be easy with them.
The ones next to a river — don't measure them at all.
phrases.notes: He means the same four-cubit strip, this time along a river.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds exceptions to the rule of careful measuring in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Strips next to a channel may be measured loosely, and strips next to a river are not measured at all.

steps.title: רב יהודה is consistent with his own view on channel and river strips
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רב יהודה's measuring rules fit another statement of his: the four אמות by a channel belong to the channel's residents, and the four אמות by a river belong to everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה follows his own reasoning. He said: the four אמות next to a channel belong to the people of the channel. The four אמות next to a river belong to everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רב יהודה's measuring advice from the last step matches another rule he said about who owns the land next to water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The strip by a channel belongs to the residents who live along it, so it still counts as someone's land and is measured, just loosely. The strip by a river belongs to everyone, so it is not part of anyone's field and is not measured at all. Both measuring rules come straight out of this ownership rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning; consistent with his other view
A water channel (a small man-made canal)
The people who live along the channel

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda follows his own reasoning,
phrases.notes: This ties back to step 21: measure the channel strip loosely, and don't measure the river strip at all.

phrases.english: for Rav Yehuda said:
The four cubits next to a channel
belong to the people of the channel.
Those next to a river belong to everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה לְטַעְמֵיהּ, דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the basis of step 21's measuring exceptions using another statement of רב יהודה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The channel strip belongs to the channel's residents; the river strip belongs to the public.

steps.title: רבי אמי orders trees cut along both riverbanks
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי announces that trees must be cleared on both sides of a river, as wide as the shoulders of the boat-pullers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי would announce: Cut down the trees along both banks of the river, as wide as the full shoulders of the men who pull the boats.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי makes a public announcement that people must clear trees from both riverbanks so the boat-pullers can walk there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the idea that the riverbank belongs to everyone. Boats were pulled upstream by men walking along the shore with ropes, and trees would block them. רבי אמי sets the width to clear: the space a puller's shoulders take up.

keyTerms.meaning: The full width of the shoulders of the boat-pullers

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami would announce:
The full width of the shoulders of the pullers
phrases.notes: The pullers are the men who walked along the shore pulling boats with ropes.

phrases.english: on both sides of the river, cut down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts into practice the public nature of the riverbank strip.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trees must be cleared along both riverbanks to the width of the pullers' shoulders.

steps.title: רב נתן בר הושעיא cuts sixteen אמות and is beaten
steps.stepSummary: רב נתן בר הושעיא ordered sixteen אמות cleared, and the people of משרוניא beat him for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נתן בר הושעיא cut down sixteen אמות. The people of משרוניא came at him and beat him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a rabbi who cleared much more than רבי אמי's measure, and the angry residents beat him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story sets up the next step. The גמרא will explain why he chose sixteen אמות and why that was a mistake.

phrases.english: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya
cut down sixteen cubits.
phrases.notes: He means he had the trees cleared to that width along the river.

phrases.english: The people of Mashronya came upon him and beat him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נָתָן בַּר הוֹשַׁעְיָא קַץ שִׁיתְּסַר אַמְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story about someone who went beyond רבי אמי's measure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clearing sixteen אמות was too much, and the landowners resisted violently.

steps.title: Why sixteen אמות was a mistake
steps.stepSummary: רב נתן בר הושעיא compared the riverbank to a רשות הרבים, which is sixteen אמות wide. The גמרא rejects that: the pullers only need room to stretch their ropes, so shoulder-width is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought it was like a רשות הרבים. But that is not right. There, in a public road, we need that whole width. Here it is only so the pullers can stretch their ropes, so the width of the pullers' shoulders is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains where רב נתן's sixteen אמות came from and then shows why his comparison does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A רשות הרבים is a full public road, and it needs sixteen אמות. The riverbank path has one small job: letting the pullers walk and pull their ropes. So the smaller measure of רבי אמי is correct, and clearing more harmed the owners for no reason.

keyTerms.meaning: A public road or area, which is sixteen אמות wide
But it is not so (rejects the reasoning just given)

steps.whatToRemember: The riverbank path only needs shoulder-width for the boat-pullers, not the sixteen אמות of a רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: He thought it was like a public domain,
but it is not so:
there we need all this width,
here it is only so they can stretch their ropes,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and others have the word in square brackets. Both mean 'their ropes.'

phrases.english: so the full width of the pullers' shoulders is enough.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא סָבַר כִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים, וְלָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and rejects the reasoning behind the action in step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects comparing the riverbank path to a רשות הרבים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The riverbank path serves only the pullers' ropes, so it does not need a public road's full sixteen-אמה width.

steps.title: רבה בר רב הונא waits for his neighbors to cut first
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא owned a forest on a riverbank. When asked to cut it, he said his upstream and downstream neighbors should cut first, and then he would cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא had a forest on the bank of a river. People said to him: Let the master cut it down! He said to them: Let those above me and below me cut first, and then I will cut.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells another story: a great rabbi was asked to clear his riverbank, and he said he would do it only after his neighbors did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clearing one stretch of the riverbank does not help if the stretches before and after it are still blocked. This story sets up the challenge in the next step: shouldn't a rabbi act first himself?

keyTerms.meaning: A forest or grove of trees
On the bank of the river
Those above and those below (upstream and downstream neighbors)

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא אִבָּא אַגּוּדָּא דְנַהֲרָא,
phrases.english: had a certain forest on the bank of a river.
They said to him: Let the master cut it down!
He said to them: Let those above and below cut first,
phrases.notes: He means the owners upstream and downstream from him along the river.

phrases.english: and then I will cut.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא אִבָּא אַגּוּדָּא דְנַהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about following רבי אמי's rule to clear riverbanks.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה בר רב הונא made his own cutting depend on his neighbors cutting first.

steps.title: Shouldn't he fix himself before others?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר רב הונא: the פסוק 'התקוששו וקושו', as explained by ריש לקיש, teaches that you must fix yourself first and only then fix others.
steps.simpleTranslation: How could he act this way? It is written: 'Gather yourselves and gather,' and ריש לקיש explained: Fix yourself first, and afterward fix others!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה בר רב הונא's behavior, because a person is supposed to do the right thing himself before demanding it from others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש reads the word קשט (to adorn or improve) into the פסוק's 'קושו'. So a person must first improve himself and only then others. רבה בר רב הונא seems to do the opposite by waiting for his neighbors to act first.

phrases.english: How could he act this way?
But isn't it written: "Gather yourselves together, and gather",
phrases.notes: צפניה 2:1

phrases.english: and Reish Lakish said:
Adorn yourself first,
phrases.notes: ריש לקיש is playing on the sound of the פסוק's word, reading it as קשט, to fix up or adorn.

phrases.english: and afterward adorn others!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the behavior described in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר רב הונא's refusal to cut until his neighbors cut.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ריש לקיש's reading of the פסוק requires a person to fix himself before others, but he waited for others first.

steps.title: The neighbor was a powerful Persian officer
steps.stepSummary: The neighboring forest belonged to the house of פרזק, a Persian general. רבה בר רב הונא reasoned that if they did not cut, his cutting alone would be useless, since the pullers would get stuck at the officer's trees anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the forest belonged to the house of פרזק the general. He said: If they cut, I will cut. If they do not cut, why should I cut? For if the pullers can stretch their ropes, they will get by with their ropes...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the neighbor was a powerful officer who would not listen, so cutting his own trees alone would accomplish nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש's rule means you should not demand of others what you have not done yourself. Here the problem was different: cutting only his own stretch would not open the path, because the officer's trees would still block the pullers. So waiting was not hypocrisy; it was simply avoiding a pointless loss. The explanation continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: פרזק the general, a Persian officer
They get along, they manage to pass

steps.confusionAlert: רבה בר רב הונא is not arguing with ריש לקיש's rule. He is saying that in this case his cutting would not help anyone, so the rule does not apply.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם אִבָּא דְּבֵי פַרְזַק רוּפִילָא הֲוָה,
phrases.english: There, it was the forest of the house of Parzak the general,
and he said: If they cut, I will cut,
and if they do not cut, why should I cut?
For if they can stretch them,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the pullers' ropes.

phrases.english: they can get along with their ropes,

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם אִבָּא דְּבֵי פַרְזַק רוּפִילָא הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the circumstances: cutting alone would be pointless
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה בר רב הונא was asking others to act before he acted himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the powerful officer would not cut, his own cutting would not help the pullers, so waiting was reasonable.
